title: Scientists Found Blood Cells Inside a 115-Million-Year-Old Dinosaur

scenes.text: This dinosaur's blood survived 115 million years.
Aratasaurus, a meat-eater from northeastern Brazil. Inside the canals of its leg bones: red blood cells, turned to mineral.
Each cell is about 23 micrometres long. And they still carry heme, the iron molecule that makes blood red.
A manganese mineral, hausmannite, locked them in place after the animal was buried fast, with almost no oxygen.
Published in PNAS in November 2026 by a Curtin University team, who called it a landmark discovery.
Not blood you could pour. But molecules of it, 115 million years on. The rule that they can't last that long just broke.

description:
In November 2026, a Curtin University-led team reported mineralised red blood cells inside the vascular canals of a 115-million-year-old theropod, Aratasaurus museunacionali, from northeastern Brazil.
The cells, about 23 by 20 micrometres, carry intact heme molecules and collagen amino acids, preserved by the manganese mineral hausmannite. The paper appeared in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
What else could still be hiding inside old bones?
subject: theropod dinosaur fossil
first_comment: Heme molecules, 115 million years old. What should scientists look for in fossils next?
